title: RAII and the Rule of Three
summary: **RAII**: tie every resource to an object's lifetime. Acquire it in the constructor and release it in the destructor, and clean-up becomes automatic on every path. **Rule of Three**: a class that needs a destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment operator almost certainly needs all three.
markdown:
## The most important idea in C++ The language guarantees that an object's destructor runs when its lifetime ends, however that comes about. **RAII** puts that guarantee to work: a resource is acquired in a constructor and released in the matching destructor. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Constructor
open, allocate,
lock, connect"] --> U["Use the object"] --> D["Destructor
close, release,
unlock, disconnect"] U -->|"early return"| D U -->|"exception"| D U -->|"end of scope"| D ``` The name stands for "Resource Acquisition Is Initialization". It is an awkward name for a simple idea: **an object owns the resource, and the object's lifetime is the resource's lifetime**. ### Without RAII ```cpp void save() { std::FILE* file{ std::fopen("save.txt", "w") }; if (!ready()) { return; // the file is never closed } write(file); // if this throws, the file is never closed std::fclose(file); } ``` Every exit path needs its own clean-up, and every future edit to the function has to remember that. ### With RAII ```cpp class File { public: File(const char* path, const char* mode) : m_file{ std::fopen(path, mode) } {} ~File() { if (m_file) { std::fclose(m_file); } } File(const File&) = delete; File& operator=(const File&) = delete; std::FILE* get() const { return m_file; } private: std::FILE* m_file{}; }; void save() { File file{ "save.txt", "w" }; if (!ready()) { return; // closed automatically } write(file.get()); // closed even if this throws } ``` The clean-up is written once, in the destructor, and cannot be skipped. ## RAII is everywhere in the library You have been relying on it throughout the course. | Resource | RAII type | |---|---| | A block of heap memory | `std::vector`, `std::string` | | A single heap object | `std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr` | | A file | `std::ifstream`, `std::ofstream` | | A lock on a mutex | `std::lock_guard`, `std::scoped_lock` | | A thread | `std::jthread` | A "resource" is anything that must be handed back: memory, files, locks, network connections, even a temporary change of state such as a console colour. ## The Rule of Three ``` If a class needs ONE of these, it almost certainly needs ALL THREE: ┌────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐ │ ~T() │ T(const T&) │ T& operator=(const T&) │ │ destructor │ copy constructor │ copy assignment │ └────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘ ``` The reasoning is short. Writing a destructor means the class manages a resource. If it manages a resource, the compiler-generated shallow copies are wrong ([[7.03 Copy Semantics — Shallow vs Deep]]). So you must either define the two copy operations or delete them, as `File` does. | You wrote | And left the others to the compiler | Result | |---|---|---| | A destructor only | Shallow copy constructor and assignment | Double delete on the first copy | | Destructor and copy constructor | Shallow assignment | Double delete on the first `b = a` | These five special functions are together called the **special member functions** (the five here plus the two move operations in the next lesson, which turn this into the **Rule of Five**). ## The Rule of Zero The better rule is to need none of them. ```cpp class Playlist { private: std::string m_name{}; std::vector m_songs{}; std::unique_ptr m_cover{}; }; ``` Every member already manages its own resource. The compiler-generated destructor, copies and moves are therefore correct, and `Playlist` declares no special member functions at all. That is the **Rule of Zero**. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q{"Does this class directly manage
a raw resource?"} -- "no (almost always)" --> Z["Rule of Zero:
write no special members"] Q -- "yes: a small, dedicated
wrapper class" --> F["Rule of Three / Five:
write or delete all of them"] ``` The design this leads to: a handful of small classes whose **only** job is to wrap one raw resource, and everything else built from them with no manual management at all. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why does RAII prevent leaks when an exception is thrown? - Exceptions cannot be thrown from RAII objects + Leaving each scope runs the local objects' destructors - The operating system releases everything as soon as an exception starts - RAII classes catch every exception > Leaving a scope by any route, return or exception, runs local destructors. RAII puts the clean-up in those destructors. ? What does the Rule of Zero say? - A class should have no member variables - Never write a constructor + Write no destructor or copy/move: let members manage themselves - Every pointer member should start as `nullptr` > If members like `std::vector` and `std::unique_ptr` manage the resources, the compiler-generated operations are already right. ? Why does needing a destructor imply needing the copy operations? - Because the compiler cannot generate copies for classes with destructors - Because destructors are only called on copies - It does not; the two are unrelated + A destructor means the class owns a resource, and the default member-by-member copy would leave two owners > That is the Rule of Three: a destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment come together, or copying must be forbidden. ? What does RAII tie together? - A pointer and the variable it points at + A resource's lifetime and its owning object's lifetime - The constructor and the copy constructor - The stack and the heap > The constructor acquires the resource and the destructor releases it, so the resource lives exactly as long as its owner. ```
ideas:
1. Write a `Timer` RAII class that prints the elapsed time in its destructor, and wrap blocks of code with it.
2. Write a `ConsoleColor` RAII class that switches the text colour in its constructor and restores it in its destructor.
3. Take a class that holds a raw `int*` array, change the member to a `std::vector<int>`, and delete all its special member functions.

cards.a:
Write no destructor or copy/move: let members manage themselves

cards.q: Why does needing a destructor imply needing the copy operations?
cards.a:
A destructor means the class owns a resource, and the default member-by-member copy would leave two owners

That is the Rule of Three: a destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment come together, or copying must be forbidden.

A resource's lifetime and its owning object's lifetime

The constructor acquires the resource and the destructor releases it, so the resource lives exactly as long as its owner.
